title: Insulin and the Quarrel over Credit
topic: the discovery of insulin and the dispute over credit
paragraphs: When news of the 1923 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine reached Toronto, one of the two winners reacted not with joy but with anger.
Frederick Banting learned that he would share the prize with John James Rickard Macleod, the professor of physiology in whose Toronto department the work had been done.
Banting considered refusing it.

Instead he announced that he would split his prize money with Charles Best, the student who had worked beside him, and Macleod responded by splitting his with James Collip, the biochemist who had purified the extract.
The record supports a less dramatic conclusion than the legend: insulin was the product of a team, and the instruments we use to assign credit were never built to describe one.

The trail begins in 1869, when Paul Langerhans, a medical student in Berlin, described small clusters of cells scattered through the pancreas that looked nothing like the surrounding tissue, which makes digestive juice for the gut.
He did not know what the clusters did, and he did not guess.

In 1889, at Strasbourg, Oskar Minkowski and Joseph von Mering removed the pancreas from a dog and found that the animal developed every sign of diabetes, including urine so rich in sugar that it drew flies.

In 1893 the French histologist Edouard Laguesse named the clusters the islets of Langerhans and proposed that they released something directly into the blood, an internal secretion in the language of the day.

A name came before a substance: the Belgian Jean de Meyer proposed insuline in 1909, and the English physiologist Edward Sharpey-Schafer proposed it again in 1916, both from the Latin insula, meaning island.
Extracting the hormone was harder than naming it, because injected pancreas extracts often caused fever, abscesses, and toxic reactions.
Georg Zuelzer in Berlin treated diabetic patients with a pancreatic extract around 1908 and saw their sugar fall before side effects forced him to stop.
Ernest Scott in Chicago in 1912 and Israel Kleiner in New York in 1919 each lowered the blood sugar of depancreatized dogs with extracts, and each stopped short of treating a patient.
Nicolae Paulescu in Bucharest reported in 1921 that his extract lowered the blood sugar of diabetic dogs, publishing in French months before the Toronto results appeared.
It is sobering that the substance sat in impure form in several laboratories for more than a decade before anyone could keep a patient alive with it.

In the autumn of 1920 Banting was a struggling surgeon in London, Ontario, preparing a lecture on the pancreas, when he read an article about a patient whose pancreatic duct had been blocked by a stone.
In such cases the enzyme-producing tissue of the gland withers while the islets survive.
Early on October 31 he wrote himself a note: tie off the pancreatic ducts of dogs, wait for the digestive tissue to degenerate, and extract whatever the surviving islets contained.
His reasoning was that earlier extracts had failed because the gland's own digestive enzymes destroyed the hormone during preparation.
He took the idea to Macleod, an authority on carbohydrate metabolism, who was skeptical but agreed to provide laboratory space, ten dogs, and a student assistant for the summer of 1921.
The assistant was Charles Best, a twenty-two-year-old with a fresh degree in physiology and biochemistry who could measure blood sugar in small samples, a skill Banting lacked.
The two began on May 17, 1921; Macleod left for Scotland in June, an absence Banting never let him forget.
On July 30, 1921, an extract of duct-ligated pancreas was injected into a depancreatized dog, and its blood sugar fell.
Banting and Best called the material isletin.

Over the following months they found that extracts of fetal calf pancreas worked, and then that whole adult beef pancreas soaked in alcohol worked too; it was the alcohol method that made the slow business of duct ligation unnecessary.
Banting's hypothesis had been the doorway rather than the destination; the method that finally mattered was close to what Scott had tried a decade earlier.
When Macleod returned in September he pressed for better controls and repeated experiments, advice that Banting took as interference.
In December Macleod brought in Collip, a biochemist from the University of Alberta on sabbatical in Toronto.
Collip's contribution was purification.
By precipitating the extract in rising concentrations of alcohol he found that the active substance came out of solution near ninety percent while most contaminating protein stayed in solution.

He also showed that the extract made the liver store glycogen and that an overdose in rabbits produced convulsions that a dose of sugar could reverse, an early description of what would be called insulin shock.
The first patient was Leonard Thompson, a fourteen-year-old boy who weighed about sixty-five pounds and was dying of diabetes in Toronto General Hospital.
On January 11, 1922, he received an injection of the Banting and Best extract.
His blood sugar fell somewhat, but sugar remained in his urine and a sterile abscess formed at the injection site; by any honest reading, the first trial failed.
On January 23 he received Collip's purified extract.
His blood sugar dropped sharply, the sugar in his urine nearly vanished, and the ketones that mark a body consuming its own fat disappeared.
Thompson lived another thirteen years.
Success did not bring peace.
Within days of the second injection Collip told Banting and Best that he would not share his purification method, and an argument followed that, by the participants' later accounts, turned physical.
On January 25 the four signed an agreement to work together under Macleod's direction and to seek no patents independently.
Then the method failed: when Collip tried to make larger batches the extract lost its potency, and for weeks no one in Toronto could produce usable insulin.
Best recovered a working process in May.
That same month the university reached an agreement with Eli Lilly and Company of Indianapolis to produce insulin at scale.
The patent question showed the group at its best.
Banting at first refused to put his name on any patent, holding that a physician should not profit from a remedy, so Best and Collip filed the application and his name was added later.
In 1923 the three assigned the United States patent to the Board of Governors of the University of Toronto for one dollar each.

The purpose was not income but control: the university could license manufacturers, require that every batch meet a standard of potency and purity, and keep any one company from cornering a drug that patients would need every day for life.
Whatever one makes of the men's quarrels, this decision was made with patients in view.
The Nobel committee acted quickly, partly because the Danish physiologist August Krogh, himself a laureate, visited Toronto in late 1922, carried the method home, and nominated Banting and Macleod.
The prize was announced in October 1923.
Banting, who turned thirty-two that November, remains the youngest laureate in that category and was the first Canadian to win a Nobel Prize.
None of that softened his conviction that Macleod had taken credit for his idea, nor his insistence that Best belonged on the citation.
Macleod regarded the award as recognition of a department's achievement and quietly shared his money with the man who had made the extract safe to inject.
The two laureates never reconciled, and Macleod left Toronto for Scotland in 1928.
What, then, was discovered, and by whom?

Banting supplied the idea and the stubbornness to test it, Best the daily laboratory work, Collip the purification that turned a toxic soup into a medicine, and Macleod the laboratory, the discipline, and the standing that got the work heard.

The historian Michael Bliss, whose 1982 study remains the standard account, reached much the same verdict from the notebooks and was not gentle with the summer experiments, which contain errors a more experienced investigator would have caught.
Yet the error-prone summer led somewhere, and the careful investigators before it had not.
Prizes honor names, and history remembers names; the discovery itself was made by a laboratory.

That is less a criticism of the Nobel committee than a limit of its instrument, and the Toronto quarrel is best read not as a contest with a rightful winner but as four men learning that a shared achievement cannot be divided.

questions.stem: According to the passage, after Banting announced that he would split his prize money with Best, Macleod
choices: refused any share of the prize
divided his own share of the prize money with Best
split his share of the money with Collip
briefly considered declining the award
publicly disputed Banting's claim to the discovery

proof.quote: Macleod responded by splitting his with James Collip

questions.why: Paragraph 1 says Macleod responded by splitting his prize money with James Collip, the biochemist who had purified the extract.
distractorNotes: Macleod accepted the prize; nothing in the passage says he refused a share.
Best received money from Banting, not from Macleod.
It was Banting who considered refusing the prize, not Macleod.
The passage never says Macleod publicly disputed Banting's claim.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the 1889 experiment of Minkowski and von Mering showed that
choices: a dog without its pancreas developed diabetes
the islets release an internal secretion
the pancreas makes digestive juice
sugar in the urine could be reversed by a pancreatic extract
a stone blocking the pancreatic duct destroys the islets

proof.quote: removed the pancreas from a dog and found that the animal developed every sign of diabetes

questions.why: Paragraph 2 says that at Strasbourg in 1889 Minkowski and von Mering removed a dog's pancreas and the animal developed every sign of diabetes.
distractorNotes: The islet idea was Laguesse's proposal in 1893, not a result of the 1889 experiment.
Digestive juice is mentioned in describing Langerhans's work, not as a finding of this experiment.
No extract was given in 1889; the experiment removed the organ and watched diabetes appear.
The duct stone appears in paragraph 4, and there the islets survive rather than being destroyed.

questions.stem: The author mentions the flies in paragraph 2 primarily to
choices: explain Laguesse's internal secretion idea
suggest the laboratory was poorly kept
show that Langerhans's clusters had a digestive function
make vivid how much sugar the dog's urine carried
contrast the dog's condition with that of Leonard Thompson

proof.quote: including urine so rich in sugar that it drew flies

questions.why: The flies are a concrete picture of the sign named in the same sentence: urine so rich in sugar that it drew flies. The detail makes the dog's diabetes visible.
distractorNotes: Laguesse's 1893 proposal is a separate sentence and is not tied to the flies.
The passage says nothing about the state of the laboratory.
The clusters are set apart from the digestive tissue, and the flies illustrate sugar loss, not digestion.
Thompson appears in paragraph 7 and is never compared with the dog.

questions.stem: All of the following are named in the passage as investigators whose pancreatic extracts lowered sugar before 1922 EXCEPT:
choices: Georg Zuelzer
Ernest Scott
Israel Kleiner
Nicolae Paulescu
Paul Langerhans

proof.quote: Georg Zuelzer in Berlin treated diabetic patients with a pancreatic extract around 1908 and saw their sugar fall
Ernest Scott in Chicago in 1912 and Israel Kleiner in New York in 1919 each lowered the blood sugar of depancreatized dogs with extracts
Israel Kleiner in New York in 1919 each lowered the blood sugar of depancreatized dogs with extracts
Nicolae Paulescu in Bucharest reported in 1921 that his extract lowered the blood sugar of diabetic dogs
He did not know what the clusters did, and he did not guess.

questions.why: Paragraph 3 confirms Zuelzer, Scott, Kleiner, and Paulescu one by one. Langerhans, in paragraph 2, described the clusters in 1869 and did not even guess what they did; he made no extract.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 3 says Zuelzer treated patients with an extract and saw their sugar fall.
Paragraph 3 says Scott lowered the blood sugar of depancreatized dogs in 1912.
Paragraph 3 says Kleiner did the same in New York in 1919.
Paragraph 3 says Paulescu reported his extract lowered blood sugar in diabetic dogs in 1921.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that, by 1921, the chief obstacle to treating diabetes with a pancreatic extract was
choices: ignorance of which organ controlled blood sugar
the impurity of the extracts rather than their absence
the lack of a name for the hormone being sought
the refusal of physicians to test extracts on patients
the absence of a reliable way to make a diabetic animal

proof.quote: injected pancreas extracts often caused fever, abscesses, and toxic reactions
the substance sat in impure form in several laboratories for more than a decade

questions.why: Paragraph 3 says the extracts caused fever, abscesses, and toxic reactions, and the author adds that the substance sat in impure form in several laboratories for more than a decade. The problem was purity, not existence.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 2 says the 1889 experiment had already tied the pancreas to diabetes.
The name insuline existed by 1909, before the substance was isolated.
Zuelzer did treat patients; what stopped him was side effects, not refusal.
Removing the pancreas was already a known way to produce diabetes in a dog.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Banting proposed tying off the pancreatic ducts of dogs because he believed that
choices: the islets would multiply once the ducts closed
Macleod had suggested the procedure
stones in the pancreatic duct were the usual cause of diabetes in people
the gland's own enzymes were destroying the hormone
duct ligation was the only way to obtain a usable extract

proof.quote: earlier extracts had failed because the gland's own digestive enzymes destroyed the hormone during preparation

questions.why: Paragraph 4 gives his reasoning directly: earlier extracts had failed because the gland's own digestive enzymes destroyed the hormone during preparation, so letting that tissue degenerate first should protect it.
distractorNotes: The passage says the islets survive when the duct is blocked, not that they multiply.
Macleod was skeptical of the idea; it was Banting's, not his.
The stone case was the article that gave Banting the idea; the passage never calls stones the usual cause of diabetes.
Paragraph 5 says duct ligation turned out to be unnecessary, so it was not the only way.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which finding made duct ligation unnecessary?
choices: Whole adult beef pancreas soaked in alcohol gave a working extract
Extracts of fetal calf pancreas lowered blood sugar in dogs
Collip's alcohol precipitation removed the contaminating protein
Blood sugar could be measured in small samples
Macleod's demand for repeated experiments confirmed the summer results

proof.quote: it was the alcohol method that made the slow business of duct ligation unnecessary

questions.why: Paragraph 5 says whole adult beef pancreas soaked in alcohol worked, and that it was the alcohol method that made duct ligation unnecessary.
distractorNotes: Fetal calf pancreas worked, but the passage credits the alcohol method, not the fetal extracts, with ending duct ligation.
Collip's precipitation is in paragraph 6 and concerns purifying the extract, not how the gland was prepared.
Measuring blood sugar was Best's skill; it does not touch the duct question.
Macleod's demands are in paragraph 6 and are never linked to duct ligation.

questions.stem: The author mentions the rabbit experiments in paragraph 6 primarily to
choices: explain why Collip refused to share his method
show that Collip's work went beyond purification
argue that the extract was too dangerous to give to patients
illustrate why the first Thompson injection failed
demonstrate that Macleod's demand for controls was justified

proof.quote: Collip's contribution was purification.
He also showed that the extract made the liver store glycogen and that an overdose in rabbits produced convulsions

questions.why: Paragraph 6 states that Collip's contribution was purification, then opens the next sentence with "He also showed," adding the glycogen and overdose findings. The rabbits extend his contribution past purification.
distractorNotes: Collip's refusal is in paragraph 8 and is never explained by the rabbits.
The passage goes straight on to treat a patient; it does not argue the extract was too dangerous.
The first injection failed through impurity and an abscess, not an overdose.
Macleod's demand for controls is a separate sentence about Banting's resentment.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the injection Leonard Thompson received on January 11, 1922
choices: used the extract that Collip had purified
cleared the ketones from his urine within a day
lowered his blood sugar sharply but produced convulsions and coma
had no measurable effect on his blood sugar
lowered his blood sugar only somewhat and caused an abscess

proof.quote: His blood sugar fell somewhat, but sugar remained in his urine and a sterile abscess formed at the injection site

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says his blood sugar fell somewhat, sugar remained in his urine, and a sterile abscess formed at the injection site. That was January 11; the sharp drop came on January 23.
distractorNotes: Collip's purified extract was the second injection, on January 23.
The ketones disappeared after the January 23 injection, not the first.
The sharp drop belongs to January 23, and no convulsions are reported in Thompson.
The passage says his blood sugar fell somewhat, so there was a measurable effect.

questions.stem: The passage implies that the agreement signed on January 25, 1922 was a response to
choices: Macleod's return from Scotland the previous September
the loss of potency in Collip's larger batches
the dispute over Collip's purification method
the university's negotiations with Eli Lilly
Banting's refusal to put his name on a patent

proof.quote: Collip told Banting and Best that he would not share his purification method
signed an agreement to work together under Macleod's direction and to seek no patents independently

questions.why: Paragraph 8 places the agreement right after Collip's refusal to share his method and the argument that followed, and its terms, working together and seeking no patents independently, answer exactly that dispute.
distractorNotes: Macleod's return is in paragraph 6, months earlier, and is not connected to the agreement.
The batches lost potency after the agreement; the passage says "Then the method failed."
The Lilly arrangement came in May, after the agreement.
Banting's refusal concerns the patent application in paragraph 9, which came later.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the inventors assigned the patent to the University of Toronto for all of the following reasons EXCEPT to
choices: keep control over the drug in the university's hands
license the companies that manufactured insulin
require that every batch meet a standard of potency and purity
provide the university with a steady source of income
prevent any one company from cornering the drug

proof.quote: The purpose was not income but control
the university could license manufacturers
require that every batch meet a standard of potency and purity
keep any one company from cornering a drug
The purpose was not income but control

questions.why: Paragraph 9 says the purpose was not income but control, then lists licensing manufacturers, batch standards of potency and purity, and keeping any one company from cornering the drug. Income is the one the passage rules out.
distractorNotes: Control is named outright as the purpose in paragraph 9.
Licensing manufacturers is the first item in the list.
The potency and purity standard is the second item.
Keeping any one company from cornering the drug is the third item.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 9, the word "cornering" most nearly means
choices: trapping
monopolizing
turning
cheapening
discontinuing

proof.quote: keep any one company from cornering a drug that patients would need every day for life

questions.why: The sentence is about keeping any one company from controlling a drug that patients need every day. To corner a market is to monopolize it, which fits; trapping is the word's everyday sense and does not.
distractorNotes: Trapping is the everyday meaning of corner, but a company cannot trap a drug.
Turning a corner is a different idiom and makes no sense here.
Cheapening is the opposite worry; the fear was control of supply, not low prices.
Discontinuing is not suggested; the concern is one company holding the supply.

questions.stem: According to the passage, August Krogh
choices: nominated Banting and Macleod after visiting Toronto
was the first Canadian to win a Nobel Prize
shared his prize money with Collip
served as the Nobel committee's Danish chairman in 1923
published the standard historical account of the discovery

proof.quote: visited Toronto in late 1922, carried the method home, and nominated Banting and Macleod

questions.why: Paragraph 10 says Krogh, a Danish physiologist and laureate, visited Toronto in late 1922, carried the method home, and nominated Banting and Macleod.
distractorNotes: Banting was the first Canadian laureate; Krogh was Danish.
Macleod shared his money with Collip, not Krogh.
The passage calls him a laureate who nominated the pair, not a committee chairman.
The standard account is Michael Bliss's 1982 study, in paragraph 11.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the Nobel committee's decision to honor Banting and Macleod is best described as
choices: openly contemptuous of its unfairness
wholehearted agreement with its choice
measured, blaming the instrument rather than the committee
indifferent to who received the money
nostalgic for an era when scientific prizes were less bitterly contested

proof.quote: That is less a criticism of the Nobel committee than a limit of its instrument
Prizes honor names, and history remembers names; the discovery itself was made by a laboratory.

questions.why: Paragraph 11 says the problem is less a criticism of the Nobel committee than a limit of its instrument, right after noting that prizes honor names while the discovery was made by a laboratory. That is a measured judgment, not an attack.
distractorNotes: The author explicitly declines to criticize the committee; contempt is far too strong.
The author says a prize cannot represent a team discovery, so this is not wholehearted agreement.
The whole final paragraph weighs who deserves credit; the author is not indifferent.
Nothing in the passage looks back to an earlier era of prizes.

questions.stem: Which of the following situations best illustrates the author's point in the final paragraph about prizes and shared achievements?
choices: Two chemists working independently in different countries isolate the same compound and are jointly honored by a scientific society
A runner who wins a marathon gives her medal to the coach who trained her and to the club that sponsored her
A company lists every one of its three hundred employees as co-inventors on a single patent application
A student submits a teammate's results under his own name and is later exposed by the laboratory director
An award names two project leaders, though the result depended equally on an unnamed tester and designer

proof.quote: Prizes honor names, and history remembers names; the discovery itself was made by a laboratory.
a shared achievement cannot be divided

questions.why: The final paragraph says prizes honor names while the discovery was made by a laboratory. An award that names two leaders and leaves out people the result depended on is the same mismatch in a new setting.
distractorNotes: Two independent discoverers are not a team, and here the honor names both of them.
Voluntarily passing a medal along is a personal gesture, not a limit of the award itself.
Naming everyone is the opposite of the problem; the author's point is that prizes leave essential contributors out.
Taking credit for another's work is misconduct, which the passage never discusses.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that, compared with Banting and Best, earlier investigators such as Scott and Kleiner were
choices: less honest in reporting their results
more careful in method but less successful in the end
more interested in naming the hormone than in extracting it
equally successful but denied credit by the Nobel committee
hampered mainly by the lack of a surgical assistant

proof.quote: Yet the error-prone summer led somewhere, and the careful investigators before it had not.
each stopped short of treating a patient

questions.why: Paragraph 11 contrasts the error-prone summer, which led somewhere, with the careful investigators before it, who had not gotten there; paragraph 3 says Scott and Kleiner each stopped short of treating a patient.
distractorNotes: Nothing in the passage questions anyone's honesty.
The naming was done by de Meyer and Sharpey-Schafer, not by Scott or Kleiner.
They stopped short of treating a patient, so they were not equally successful, and the committee is never said to have denied them.
The passage gives no reason tied to assistants; Best's role was blood sugar measurement, not surgery.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Banting deserved the Nobel Prize alone, and Macleod's share of it was an injustice
Collip's purification was the real discovery of insulin, and the quarrel obscured it
The discovery of insulin was delayed for decades by investigators who lacked the courage to test their extracts on patients
Insulin was a team achievement, and the quarrel over credit shows how poorly prizes represent such work
The University of Toronto's handling of the insulin patent set the standard for how universities should manage medical discoveries

proof.quote: insulin was the product of a team, and the instruments we use to assign credit were never built to describe one
the discovery itself was made by a laboratory
a shared achievement cannot be divided

questions.why: Paragraph 1 states the thesis outright, that insulin was the product of a team and that our instruments for assigning credit were never built to describe one, and paragraph 11 returns to it: the discovery was made by a laboratory, and a shared achievement cannot be divided.
distractorNotes: The author sides with no single claimant and calls the quarrel a contest without a rightful winner.
Collip's purification is one of four contributions the passage weighs, not the whole discovery.
The passage blames impurity and side effects for the delay, not a lack of courage, and Zuelzer did treat patients.
The patent is one paragraph and is praised, but it is not what the passage is about.
